Asymptotic Freedom. It is a property of quantum chromodynamics, or QCD, in which the strength of the strong nuclear force between quarks decreases as they are brought closer together or as the energy of the interaction increases. Conversely, the force strengthens as quarks separate, confining them into hadrons. This counterintuitive phenomenon was discovered in nineteen seventy-three and was revolutionary because it explained why quarks behave almost as free particles at high energies while remaining permanently bound at low energies.

The running coupling constant alpha-s decreases logarithmically as the energy scale increases, opposite to electromagnetic interactions. Gluons interact with themselves, creating self-coupling effects that cause the unusual energy dependence of the strong force. This explains why deep inelastic scattering experiments revealed that quarks inside protons behave almost freely at high collision energies. The phenomenon was predicted theoretically by Gross, Wilczek, and Politzer in nineteen seventy-three. These three scientists earned the two thousand and four Nobel Prize in Physics for this discovery.

Asymptotic freedom makes perturbative calculations possible at high energies where the coupling becomes weak, enabling precise quantum chromodynamics predictions. At low energies, the coupling constant becomes large, causing quark confinement where quarks cannot exist as free particles. It is fundamental to understanding the extreme conditions in the early universe and inside neutron stars. This phenomenon explains why quark-gluon plasma forms only at extremely high temperatures in particle colliders and in the microseconds after the Big Bang. The inverse behavior of quantum chromodynamics coupling versus quantum electrodynamics demonstrates that the strong force uniquely exhibits asymptotic freedom among the fundamental interactions. These insights connect to the theory of quantum chromodynamics itself, to gluons as self-interacting force carriers, to quarks as confined particles, and to the coupling constant expressing this asymptotic freedom mathematically.
